strategy.summary: Reproduce the descending complex-sort NaN ordering bug in NumPy (PR #31572, backport of #31557, regression from #31345) by building NumPy at buggy commit b1b77568be65 and running the updated test_sort_descending_complex_lexorder, which should fail on the buggy comparator in numpy_tag.h and pass after the fix.

system_packages: a C++ compiler toolchain (gcc or clang with C++17 support)

strategy.reproducing_test: numpy/_core/tests/test_multiarray.py::TestSortComplex::test_sort_descending_complex_lexorder (parametrized over dtype, stable, descending, random_seed), with the diff applied: im_nans = arange + complex(0, nan), re_nans = complex(nan, 0) + 1j*arange, all_nans = np.full(100, complex(nan, nan), dtype=dtype)
strategy.success_criterion: On the buggy revision b1b77568be65 the test FAILS: the descending sort places imaginary-only-NaN values before real-only-NaN values, so the ordering assertion over the real-NaN mask does not hold. On the fixed revision (with the #31557/#31572 comparator change) the same test PASSES, with real-NaN-only values sorting after imaginary-only-NaN values in descending order.
strategy.numerical_probe: Sort a small complex array containing one imaginary-only NaN element and one real-only NaN element in descending order and compare their relative positions; the buggy build puts the imaginary-only NaN first.
risks: The PR author asks reviewers to confirm the intended ordering, so the expected behaviour is not fully settled by the passages; the test encodes the fixed semantics and may be the only oracle.
Only NaN special values are involved; +/-inf, signed zero and subnormals are not mentioned in the evidence and are not planned for.
No precision or tolerance is stated; the ordering check is exact on NaN masks, so tolerance does not apply.
The specific complex dtype parameterised by the test is not named in the evidence; the test is expected to exercise complex64 and complex128 via its dtype parameter, but this is inferred.

The comparator lives in C++ (numpy_tag.h complex_type); the defect is only exercised after a compiled build, so an installed wheel or a Python-only checkout cannot reproduce it. The build must be from source at the buggy commit.

The era-constraint entries for pytest and hypothesis are unbounded with no documented constraint; this plan chooses the current versions available at build time and does not pin them, since neither is numerically relevant.
The listed test_command in the environment (numpy.test()) is a generic test runner and does not select the relevant test, so it is replaced by a targeted pytest -k invocation.
Passing on the fixed revision depends on the backport being applied cleanly to b1b77568be65; if the fix is not present the transition cannot be observed.

oracle.reference_source: project test test_sort_descending_complex_lexorder in numpy/_core/tests/test_multiarray.py, as updated by PR #31572
oracle.why: NaN placement in sort order is a discrete ordering check, not a floating-point value comparison, so an exact mask-based assertion applies.

strategy.fails_on_buggy: On b1b77568be65 the comparator returns the wrong result for imaginary-only versus real-only NaN pairs in descending mode, so the sorted array places imaginary-only NaNs before real-only NaNs and the test's ordering assertion over the real-NaN mask fails.
strategy.passes_on_fixed: With the comparator changed to 'if (ra > rb)', 'if (ra < rb)' and 'return rb != rb;', real-only NaN values sort after imaginary-only NaN values in descending order and the test assertion holds for all parametrised dtype, stable and descending combinations.
